Prevention: Avoid using sprinkler irrigation as the development of the disease is greatly exacerbated under sprinklers.
Plough or remove infected residues and volunteer beans to reduce initial inoculum sources.
However, if few to no insect pests and no major diseases are in your crop, then leave residues and do not plough to improve the soil, and to reduce water evaporation.
Before planting, solarize the soil by covering it with transparent polyethylene sheets or another plastic material during sunny weather.
Leave for 20-60 days to reduce bacterial populations.
Do not mulch old bean straw from infected crops on new fields to be used for bean production.
Do not enter the bean field when plants are wet to avoid spreading the disease to unaffected areas.
Clean and disinfect equipment used in infected fields before moving to disease-free fields.
Practice crop rotation with cereals such as wheat, barley, oat and maize for three or more years.
Intercrop beans with maize to reduce the spread of infection.
Monitoring: Halo blight is a disease caused by bacteria which affects many types of beans.
Check for symtpoms of the disease at least once a week, from 2 weeks until maturing stage, particularly if conditions are favourable (cool (16-23 °C) and moist):
Leaves: small water-soaked spots (resembling pinpricks) on the undersides of the leaves that later turn red-brown and necrotic in a few days.
Often, the tissue surrounding the necrotic lesion frequently gradually becomes lime- green/yellow, forming a halo.
Pods: water-soaked, greasy spots that vary in size and may develop brown margins as they mature.
No development of halos around pod lesions, but a whitish bacterial ooze appears in the centres of the spots when wet.
Stems: may produce typical greasy spots.
Seeds: may rot or appear shrivelled and discoloured.
If infection results from seed contamination, the whole plant may exhibit a general lime-green colour, is often stunted or distorted, may have lesions around the stem, and will die early.
Consider taking action when there are more than 5-10 spots on one plant within an area of 5 square metres.
Direct Control: Remove infected plants and destroy by burning or burying to at least 60 cm.
Deep plough infested plant debris into the soil (to at least 60 cm) shortly after harvest and thoroughly cover to allow quick decomposition.
